text: Dependabot, Secret Scanning, Code Scanning, and Private Advisories: Who this is for: Anyone contributing to open source repositories needs to understand how GitHub protects code and what security alerts mean. This appendix explains the GitHub Security and quality tab, how to interpret and respond to alerts, and how to responsibly report vulnerabilities - including in community-access/accessibility-agents.

speaker: ALEX
text: A solid pull request habit is to separate three questions: what changed, why it changed, and what still needs review. That keeps the conversation useful instead of noisy.

text: A solid navigation habit is to prove where you are before activating controls. Headings, landmarks, and the address bar are not trivia; they are your map.

speaker: ALEX
text: every GitHub repository has a Security and quality tab in its navigation bar. What you see there depends on whether you are a contributor with elevated access or a public viewer.

speaker: ALEX
text: On the ground, that means a few things. Use G then S (GitHub keyboard shortcut) to jump directly to the Security and quality tab from any repo page -- much faster than Tab-navigating the full nav bar. The Security and quality tab content varies by your access level -- public viewers see only the security policy and vulnerability reporting form; contributors with write access see alerts. Dependabot alerts, secret scanning alerts, and code scanning alerts are each a separate link inside the Security and quality tab -- use K to navigate between them. The Security and quality tab link sits in the repository's top navigation bar alongside Code, Issues, PRs, and Actions -- zoom in if the tab labels are small. Alert severity badges (Critical, High, Medium, Low) use colored labels -- each badge also includes the severity word, so color is not the only indicator. If the Security and quality tab shows "No alerts," that is good news -- look for the green shield icon next to the tab name as confirmation.

speaker: JAMIE
text: If I am listening before the workshop starts, what should settle in my mind first?

speaker: ALEX
text: dependabot is GitHub's automated dependency monitoring and update system.

speaker: ALEX
text: Put Dependabot Alerts into plain language. When a known security vulnerability (CVE - Common Vulnerability and Exposure) is discovered in a package your project depends on, GitHub creates a Dependabot alert.

speaker: ALEX
text: What to do as a contributor when you see an alert.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 4 checks: Read the advisory to understand the vulnerability scope; Check whether the project actually uses the vulnerable code path; The fix is almost always: update the dependency to the fixed version; and Dependabot Security Updates may have already opened a PR - check the PRs tab.

speaker: ALEX
text: Before the learner moves on. If enabled, Dependabot automatically opens a PR to update the vulnerable dependency. As a contributor with access, reviewing and merging these Dependabot PRs is a high-value, low-risk way to contribute.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Give me the version that sounds like an instructor, not a manual.

speaker: ALEX
text: Dependabot Version Updates: Beyond security fixes, Dependabot can be configured to open PRs keeping all dependencies at their latest versions (not just security fixes). This is configured in.github/dependabot.yml.

speaker: ALEX
text: Secret scanning detects if you accidentally commit tokens, API keys, passwords, or other credentials to a repository.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where do you want a learner to place their attention here?

speaker: ALEX
text: push Protection intercepts a git push before it reaches GitHub and blocks it if it detects a known secret pattern.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is the kind of detail that keeps a screen reader user oriented.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. The named thing - the heading, tab, field, branch, or button - is the handhold.

speaker: ALEX
text: Best practice: Use environment variables for secrets, never hardcode them. The durable skill is not memorizing one screen. It is knowing how to find your footing when the screen changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of this as 3 checks: Remove the secret from the file immediately; Rotate the exposed credential (GitHub will automatically revoke detected GitHub tokens); and If it was a false positive, you can bypass with justification - but investigate first. That small check between steps is what makes the workflow reliable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Secret Scanning Alerts. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: For public repositories, GitHub scans all existing commits and creates alerts for any detected secrets. These appear in Security → Secret scanning.

speaker: ALEX
text: The next point gives the learner a handle. Learning Cards: Secret Scanning.

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where the lesson becomes something you can check. If your git push is blocked with "GH013: Repository rule violations found," the terminal output lists the exact file, line number, and secret type -- read the error lines carefully. After removing the secret from your code, use environment variables instead (process.env.GITHUB TOKEN) -- your screen reader will confirm the variable name in the code. Secret scanning alerts appear under Security and quality tab, Secret scanning -- navigate with T to reach the alert table, then arrow keys to read each row. Push Protection error messages appear in your terminal with red text -- increase terminal font size to read the file path, line number, and secret type clearly. The secret scanning alert list in the Security and quality tab uses a table layout -- zoom in to read the Secret type and Location columns. Environment variable names in code (like process.env.GITHUB TOKEN) are easier to spot when syntax highlighting is enabled in your editor theme.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on 4. Code Scanning and CodeQL. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: code scanning uses static analysis to find security vulnerabilities in the code itself (not dependencies). GitHub's built-in tool is CodeQL, which understands the code's logic and can detect.

speaker: ALEX
text: A few details make that real. SQL injection risks. Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities. Path traversal issues. Insecure cryptography usage.

speaker: ALEX
text: Hold that next to this. Put Reading a Code Scanning Alert into plain language. As a contributor: Code scanning alerts are excellent, well-scoped contribution opportunities. The useful version is: Each alert shows you the exact file, line, and the data flow causing the issue. The interface gets easier when it becomes a set of named places instead of a wall of controls.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the learner is not behind if they stop there and check the page.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Pausing to verify is not a detour; it is how you keep control of the workflow.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Where to Find Code Scanning Alerts. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Security and quality tab → Code scanning → filter by severity, rule, or file.

speaker: ALEX
text: That connects to another useful point. When you discover a security vulnerability in a project, never report it as a public issue. A public issue immediately broadcasts the vulnerability to anyone who could exploit it.

speaker: ALEX
text: How to Submit a Private Report.

speaker: ALEX
text: Severity: Your assessment. Affected versions: Which versions are vulnerable. CVSS score: Optional - the Common Vulnerability Scoring System rating.

speaker: ALEX
text: First, navigate to the repository's Security and quality tab. Then, select "Report a vulnerability" (this button only appears if the maintainer has enabled private reporting). After that, fill in the form. Finally, submit - only the maintainers see your report.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on The Responsible Disclosure Process. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: The Responsible Disclosure Process.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start here: Maintainers acknowledge your report (typically within 1-7 days for active projects). Then: They may ask follow-up questions in the private advisory thread. Next: They develop and test a fix. Last: They request a CVE (Common Vulnerability and Exposure) number from GitHub. That small check between steps is what makes the workflow reliable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Before we leave The Responsible Disclosure Process, what is the practical point?

speaker: ALEX
text: They publish a new release with the fix; They publish a public security advisory - you may be credited as the reporter; and The CVE is published publicly (usually 90 days after report or after the fix is released). The sequence works because every action has a confirmation.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on What If the Maintainer Doesn't Respond? What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: if a maintainer doesn't respond within a reasonable time (30-90 days is the standard window).

speaker: ALEX
text: Send a follow-up in the private advisory thread; Contact GitHub directly if the issue is critical (GitHub can assist with coordinated disclosure); and Follow the project's SECURITY.md for their stated disclosure policy. The sequence works because every action has a confirmation.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is a useful checkpoint before anyone starts pressing keys.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Checkpoints turn uncertainty into information.

speaker: ALEX
text: Keep the thread going. The SECURITY.md File. A SECURITY.md file at the repository root defines the project's security policy. This is the part to say slowly: accessibility-agents's security policy: community-access/accessibility-agents has a SECURITY.md that points to GitHub's private advisory form.

speaker: ALEX
text: Supported versions: Which versions receive security patches. Reporting instructions: How to report a vulnerability (email, private advisory form, etc.). Response timeline: How quickly maintainers aim to respond. Disclosure policy: When the project will publish a fix publicly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Navigating to a Repository's SECURITY.md. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Navigating to a Repository's SECURITY.md.

speaker: ALEX
text: Step one is security and quality tab → Policies section → "Security policy" link. Step two is or directly: https://github.com/owner/repo/security/policy.

speaker: ALEX
text: Treat examples as spoken recipes, not decorations. You may hear something like Security and quality tab → H → "Policy" heading → Link: "Security policy" → Enter. Read the command, understand what it changes, then run it only when the repository state matches the lesson.

speaker: ALEX
text: Another way to ground it. Do not treat 7. Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) as decoration. An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of every component (libraries, packages, dependencies) in a software project. It is increasingly required by enterprise and government organizations for supply chain security compliance.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's pause on Exporting an SBOM from GitHub. What should a learner take away from it?

speaker: ALEX
text: Exporting an SBOM from GitHub.

speaker: ALEX
text: If someone is taking notes, this is the short list. Your organization requires SBOM documentation before adopting an open source dependency. You're auditing a project's complete dependency chain. You want to identify license compatibility for a commercial product.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start here: Navigate to the repository's Insights tab. Then: Select "Dependency graph". Next: Select "Export SBOM" button (top right of the Dependency graph page). Last: GitHub generates a SPDX-format JSON file listing all dependencies with their versions and licenses.

speaker: ALEX
text: This is the part worth saying out loud. Put 9. Security and Accessibility Agents into plain language. Accessibility Agents' /security-dashboard slash command gives you a quick security overview without visiting the Security and quality tab in the browser.
